newsitem.title: USA: Reno seeks to ease concern about youth violence.
newsitem.headline: Reno seeks to ease concern about youth violence.

text.p: Attorney General Janet Reno Thursday sought to ease concerns about a dramatic surge in youth violence, citing statistics that a recent drop in juvenile arrests had been greatest among those under 15.

"These numbers offer us a very good lesson -- demographics and the rising number of young people do not have to ... reflect our destiny. We do not have to face an explosion in youth crime, as some have suggested," she said.
But James Fox, a criminal justice expert at Northeastern University in Boston, said juvenile crime rates still remained high.

"It is too early to feel secure or to suggest the problem is going away," he said. "We have not solved our juvenile crime problem. (The youth violence rate) still is at a level extremely elevated, compared with 1985."

A Justice Department report released by Reno found the rate of juvenile arrests for violent crime dropped 4 percent in 1995 while the rate fell an even steeper 7 percent for juveniles between 10 and 14.
It also showed that juvenile arrests for murder decreased 14 percent in 1995 and 23 percent in 1994 while arrests for rape dropped 4 percent last year.

"Today's figures show we can make a difference," Reno said at her weekly news conference. Asked what caused the decline, she cited programmes such as mentoring that have been adopted in different cities across the country and community policing.
Covering a wide range of other issues during her regular meeting with reporters, Reno also:

-- said the Justice Department's Office of Professional Responsibility has completed its report on the way FBI agents questioned former security guard Richard Jewell in connection with the Olympics bombing.

She said the report was under review but did not say when it would be released. The report concerns whether FBI agents improperly tried to trick Jewell, who was cleared as a suspect in October, when they brought him in July to the FBI's office in Atlanta, supposedly to make a training film.
-- vowed to make a decision quickly on whether to support a legal challenge to California's recently approved ballot initiative aimed at dismantling affirmative action programmes.

"I'm trying to get it done as soon as possible because I think it is important, but I don't want to be precipitous," she said. The White House has given the Justice Department more time to consider the legal basis for a challenge.
-- declined comment on whether the death penalty would be sought for accused Unabomber Theodore Kaczynski, who has been charged in California and New Jersey in bomb attacks that killed three people.
